generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, feedback is most useful when it changes your next piece of work, not when it explains a mark. In sport management and development, a comment might say you report what the participation campaign did but do not evaluate whether it reached the target group. That comment is reviewed, interpreted into what evaluating would actually involve, articulated as a concrete action, and applied to the next report. Treated as a loop rather than a verdict, feedback is how sport students raise their work over a module.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport management students receive the same comment on a campaign evaluation: their report describes what the participation campaign did but does not evaluate whether it reached the target group.

Tom reads the comment, feels the mark is harsh, and files the report away. On the next assignment the same comment comes back. Tom reviewed the feedback but never interpreted it into an action or applied it, so nothing changed. The feedback was received, not used.

Amara reads the comment, works out what evaluating reach would look like, and writes it as a concrete action: compare participation data against the target group before judging the campaign a success. On the next report Amara does exactly that, and the comment does not return. The cycle has closed: review, interpret, articulate, apply.

Both were given the same feedback. Only Amara fed it forward, and only Amara's work improved because of it.
generatedProse.summary: The feedback cycle in the School of Sport turns comments into improvement through four stages: review, interpret, articulate and apply. Run as a self-directed loop with a growth mindset, it closes only when your next report, plan or analysis shows the change. You can now describe the cycle, judge how well a student used feedback, and plan how to feed your own feedback forward. Together with the earlier lessons, you now own the learning, assessment and feedback cycle.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara's work improve when Tom's did not?

items.text: She interpreted the comment into a concrete action and applied it to her next report.
She disagreed with the mark more strongly.
She received more detailed feedback than Tom.
She kept the feedback filed for later reference.

feedback.correct: That's right. Interpreting the comment into an action and applying it is what closed the loop and improved the work.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the same comment.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's work improved because she interpreted the comment into a concrete action and applied it. The same feedback, filed or merely disputed, changed nothing.
